code_label: QML applied to SME credit scoring
text_span: we explore the use of quantum machine learning (QML) applied to credit scoring for small and medium-sized enterprises (SME)
rationale: States the paper’s main application focus and research objective.

text_span: A quantum/classical hybrid approach has been used with several models, activation functions, epochs and other parameters.
rationale: Summarizes the experimental approach as a hybrid comparison across model settings.

text_span: Results are shown from the best model, using two quantum classifiers and a classical neural network, applied to data for companies in Singapore.
rationale: Identifies the best-performing model structure and dataset context.

text_span: the quantum model trained for 350 epochs compared to 3500 epochs for comparable prediction performance.
rationale: Reports the key training-efficiency finding.

code_label: Accuracy worsens with more qubits and blocks
text_span: a degradation in the accuracy was observed as the number of qubits was increased beyond 12 qubits and also with the addition of extra classifier blocks in the quantum model.
rationale: States an observed performance decline under scaling and added blocks.

text_span: Practical issues for executing on simulators and real quantum computers are also explored.
rationale: Signals that implementation constraints are part of the study.

text_span: Overall, we see great promise in this first in-depth exploration of the use of hybrid QML in credit scoring.
rationale: Captures the authors’ overall positive assessment.

text_span: it lacks having a class of practically useful, real-world problems where practical advantage could be obtained.
rationale: Frames the broader motivation for seeking practical quantum advantage.

code_label: Credit scoring as a finance use case
text_span: Important problems of computational finance include the risk management and the pricing of exotic derivatives using Monte-Carlo models, modelling financial markets with differential equations, credit scoring, portfolio optimization, understanding market trends with machine learning methods
rationale: Places credit scoring among major computational finance problems.

text_span: small companies are usually not covered by rating agencies and may suffer from reduced availability of credit.
rationale: Explains why SME credit scoring matters.

text_span: Currently even the best credit scoring models only reject 90% of companies that become insolvent (type II error) while rejecting 15% of companies that remain healthy (type I error)
rationale: Provides a benchmark claim about current model performance.

text_span: we focus in this paper on models previously developed by authors, the FULL HYBRID classical-quantum neural networks architecture [27], to perform supervised learning on the problem of credit scoring in finance
rationale: Identifies the specific model family used in the paper.

text_span: general performance on synthetic datasets tends to be better compared with real world datasets
rationale: Notes a comparative observation about dataset type.

text_span: The area under the ROC curve (AUC) is calculated by summing the area under each ROC curve in Figure 1 and normalising the areas to 1.0.
rationale: Defines the main evaluation metric used throughout the study.

text_span: credit scoring is typically formulated as a binary classification problem with highly imbalanced data (most companies do not default).
rationale: Describes the problem formulation and class imbalance.

code_label: Best classical model selected for Singapore data
text_span: we consider the best classical Singapore country model for classification of two groups of potential SME borrowers
rationale: States the classical comparator chosen for benchmarking.

text_span: This model achieves a score of 0.73 (see results section).
rationale: Reports the classical benchmark performance.

code_label: XGBoost not used for neural comparison
text_span: XGBoost has been found to be the best model for this dataset but, as we want to compare neural networks, this model is not used in this paper.
rationale: Explains a methodological exclusion and comparison constraint.

text_span: a FULL HYBRID (FH) quantum neural network model consisting of three different approaches based on: hybrid-neural networks, variational circuits and data-reuploading classifier
rationale: Summarizes the architecture’s three-part design.

text_span: We use a Rx gate for angle embedding in our experiments.
rationale: Specifies the quantum data-encoding choice.

text_span: By adding many blocks, we re-introduce the input data into the model.
rationale: Describes the mechanism of the data re-uploading technique.

code_label: Complementary strengths of VC and DRC
text_span: VC and DRC combined together will complement each other to get the best results.
rationale: States the authors’ expectation about combining the two quantum submodules.

text_span: The dataset originates from various Singapore institutions
rationale: Identifies the data source context.

text_span: We sampled all 246 class 1 companies in the period and added to it a random subsample of 2000 class 0 companies.
rationale: Describes how the dataset was assembled.

text_span: For the experiments, due to the limitations of the computing hardware, the maximum number of features used is 21.
rationale: States a hardware-imposed constraint on feature count.

text_span: The training dataset has 1798 rows of data split into a validation set of 180 rows (10%) and a test set of 270 rows (15%).
rationale: Specifies the data partitioning used in experiments.

text_span: Throughout the simulations, the same training, validation, and testing dataset is used.
rationale: Indicates a fixed split for all configurations.

text_span: For every configuration, we used the average outcome of ROC/AUC score of 5 simulations.
rationale: Describes the repetition and averaging protocol.

text_span: For a fair comparison, the number of epochs for quantum and classical models were kept identical at 350.
rationale: Explains the fairness constraint in training comparisons.

code_label: Classical model improves with longer training
text_span: the classical model improved if training was increased up to 5,000 epochs.
rationale: Reports a training-duration effect for the classical model.

text_span: The number of DRC blocks was increased from 1 to 10 and the number of qubits was increased from 6 to 18.
rationale: States the parameter sweep used for the quantum model.

text_span: The optimizer we used is a Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) optimizer. The loss function is binary cross-entropy
rationale: Specifies optimization and loss choices.

text_span: The quantum model achieved an ROC/AUC of 0.75
rationale: Reports the main quantum model performance.

text_span: whereas the CC model achieved an ROC/AUC of 0.73
rationale: Reports the classical counterpart performance.

code_label: Classical model matches with more epochs
text_span: letting the classical counterpart model train up to 5,000 epochs can lead to the highest score of 0.75
rationale: Shows that extended classical training can match the quantum score.

text_span: for blocks=1 (black dots) we observe that ROC/AUC increases up to 12 qubits and then decreases.
rationale: Describes the observed non-monotonic qubit-scaling behavior.

text_span: The same behaviour can also be observed when one increases the number of blocks with the highest results being achieved with no data-reupload.
rationale: Reports the effect of adding blocks on performance.

code_label: Execution time scales with qubits and blocks
text_span: data embedding time doubles with each additional qubit, model execution time scales quadratically with the number of qubits and linearly with the number of blocks
rationale: Summarizes the runtime scaling observation.

code_label: Simulator resource test up to 20 qubits
text_span: We used up to 20 qubits for this test.
rationale: States the upper bound used in the timing experiment.

text_span: the FH model required significantly less epochs to train than the CC model by a factor if 2 or more
rationale: Highlights the training-efficiency advantage claimed for the hybrid model.

code_label: Qubit increase may relate to barren plateaus
text_span: The unexpected finding that increasing the number of qubits above 12 (Fig. 3) reduced the accuracy could be related to barren plateau issues but is to be investigated in future studies.
rationale: States a possible explanation and explicitly flags future investigation.

code_label: More blocks may not help for this dataset
text_span: The effect of adding more blocks, i.e. DRC, reducing the accuracy (Fig. 3) could be due to our dataset not having features that have a trigonometric (i.e. sine) structure
rationale: Provides a dataset-specific caveat for the block-depth result.

code_label: Circuit execution burden on cloud hardware
text_span: for 350 epochs and a training set of 1798, this amounts to 629,300 circuit executions.
rationale: Quantifies the computational burden of training.

text_span: for a quantum computer accessed on a cloud platform, the overall time taken may not practical
rationale: States a practical deployment concern for cloud execution.

text_span: Qiskit runtime that enables the execution of the classical and quantum code to be run as one unit reducing the overall execution time by 120 times
rationale: Identifies a software improvement that may reduce runtime.

code_label: Larger datasets and more complex models suggested
text_span: A much larger dataset such as the UK’s with 1000+ defaults each year and over 4 million companies would be interesting to use with more complex models and finer grained risk periods.
rationale: States a concrete future research direction.

text_span: hyperparameters for the FH and CC models could potentially be tuned further.
rationale: Notes additional optimization work remains.

code_label: Hybrid models promising for fewer epochs
text_span: the use of hybrid quantum/classical models is promising given the ease of obtaining comparable results to a purely classical counterpart and with much fewer epochs for training.
rationale: Summarizes the main conclusion about promise and training efficiency.

code_label: Hardware growth may enable real advantages
text_span: with even modest improvements in hardware expected of over 4,000 qubits by 2025
rationale: Links future hardware progress to potential benefits.

text_span: the best classical model for Singapore data is still XGBoost
rationale: Acknowledges the strongest classical baseline outside the neural comparison.

text_span: the introduction of quantum noise possibly removing the need for dropout layers.
rationale: Speculates on a possible effect of moving to real hardware.
